A.text: A purpose-made circuit-breaker lockout and padlock secure the device against inadvertent operation.

B.text: Padlocking a suitable isolating switch provides the positive security that a safe isolation needs.

C.text: Removing the fuse and securing access can disconnect the circuit and prevent unauthorised replacement under the procedure.

D.text: Tape does not secure an isolating device against inadvertent or unauthorised operation. HSE construction guidance explicitly contrasts tape over a circuit-breaker with a proper lock-off device, personal lock and safety notice.

questions.prompt: Which of the following work procedures on electrical systems will always require a permit-to-work to be issued?
questions.explanation: An electrical permit-to-work should state what circuit or equipment has been made safe, how that has been achieved and what work is to be done. A permit should not, therefore, be used for live working. Such a permit is always required for work on high-voltage systems, but can also be used for low-voltage systems.

A.text: An electrical permit-to-work should state what circuit or equipment has been made safe, how that has been achieved and what work is to be done. A permit should not, therefore, be used for live working. Such a permit is always required for work on high-voltage systems, but can also be used for low-voltage systems.

B.text: Low-voltage dead work often uses secure isolation procedures, but it does not invariably require a formal permit.

C.text: High-voltage live work is exceptional and governed by specialised safety rules; a dead-work permit does not authorise it.

D.text: Low-voltage live work needs legal justification and precautions, but a permit-to-work is not automatic in every case.

questions.prompt: Optical fibre cable remnants should not be left lying around on site because:

options.A: Laser beams still exist in the cut pieces
options.C: They can be hot and burn upon contact
options.D: They can pierce the skin or eyes

questions.explanation: Fibre fragments can enter the bloodstream and cause infections in the skin or eyes. All fibre waste, particularly small pieces, should be placed in suitable receptacles.

A.text: A detached scrap of passive fibre does not retain a laser beam once it is disconnected from an active source.

B.text: Ordinary glass fibre offcuts are a sharp-injury hazard, not a toxic substance that poisons by contact.

C.text: Cable remnants do not normally stay hot; their danger is the fine, stiff shard penetrating tissue.

D.text: Fibre fragments can enter the bloodstream and cause infections in the skin or eyes. All fibre waste, particularly small pieces, should be placed in suitable receptacles.

questions.prompt: Why must a live or potentially live unterminated optical-fibre end never be viewed directly or pointed towards anyone's eyes?

options.A: The beam can bore a hole through the skin
options.B: The beam can damage the eyes
options.C: The beam can transfer a strong electric current
options.D: The colour of the beam is very hypnotic

questions.explanation: Active communications fibre can emit concentrated optical radiation, including wavelengths that are not visible. Viewing the end can focus that energy onto the retina and cause eye injury, so the link should be treated as active until proved otherwise.

A.text: Communications optical power can injure the retina but does not behave like a cutting beam boring through skin.

B.text: Active communications fibre can emit concentrated optical radiation, including wavelengths that are not visible. Viewing the end can focus that energy onto the retina and cause eye injury, so the link should be treated as active until proved otherwise.

C.text: Fibre carries light rather than a conductive electric current, so electrical transfer is not the eye hazard.

D.text: Some hazardous wavelengths are invisible; hypnosis by colour is fictional and would miss the retinal exposure risk.

questions.prompt: The use of a multi-lock hasp with the appropriate number of padlocks is a recommended method of safe isolation where:

options.A: Individual circuit breaker locking off devices are not available
options.B: Individual circuit breakers are not identified at the distribution board
options.C: More than one person will be working on circuits supplied from the same distribution board
options.D: You know the health and safety inspector is in the area

questions.explanation: A multi-lock hasp lets several workers each fit their own padlock, so the isolator cannot be switched back on until every person has finished and removed their lock. This guarantees no one is re-energised while another is still working.

A.text: The need for a hasp comes from multiple personal locks, not from the absence of a device for one circuit-breaker.

B.text: Unidentified circuits must be traced and labelled; a multi-lock hasp cannot correct uncertainty about the isolation point.

C.text: A multi-lock hasp lets several workers each fit their own padlock, so the isolator cannot be switched back on until every person has finished and removed their lock. This guarantees no one is re-energised while another is still working.

D.text: Isolation arrangements are based on people exposed to reconnection risk, not on whether an inspector is nearby.

questions.prompt: Which of the following procedures should be used when more than one person will be working on circuits supplied from a distribution board which has been switched off?

options.A: Blowing a horn before the power is switched on again
options.B: Giving each operative a volt stick
options.C: Telling everyone what time the power will be switched on again
options.D: The use of a multi-lock hasp on the isolator with a padlock for each operative

questions.explanation: With several people working from one isolated board, each fits a padlock to a multi-lock hasp so the supply stays off until everyone has finished and removed their own lock. Verbal warnings or horns rely on memory and cannot physically prevent re-energisation.

A.text: An audible warning relies on memory and hearing and gives no personal control over reconnection at the isolator.

B.text: A voltage stick cannot secure isolation or prevent another person from energising the distribution board.

C.text: An agreed time is not a lock-off; work may overrun and someone may reconnect without knowing who remains exposed.

D.text: With several people working from one isolated board, each fits a padlock to a multi-lock hasp so the supply stays off until everyone has finished and removed their own lock. Verbal warnings or horns rely on memory and cannot physically prevent re-energisation.

questions.prompt: What colour cable USUALLY signifies 110 volt power supply on site?
questions.explanation: Reduced low-voltage 110V site supplies are colour-coded yellow across cables, plugs, sockets and transformers so they are instantly recognisable. The 110V centre-tapped system limits shock voltage to around 55V to earth, making it safer for site tools.

A.text: Black is not the recognised site connector and cable identification for the 110 V reduced-low-voltage system.

B.text: Blue is associated with the 230 V range and would risk connecting equipment to the wrong nominal supply.

C.text: Red is associated with 400 V three-phase supplies, not the ordinary 110 V site-tool system.

D.text: Reduced low-voltage 110V site supplies are colour-coded yellow across cables, plugs, sockets and transformers so they are instantly recognisable. The 110V centre-tapped system limits shock voltage to around 55V to earth, making it safer for site tools.

questions.prompt: A portable electric generator on site has two power outlets, 110 volts and 230 volts. What colour would the 110 volt outlet be?
questions.explanation: The 110V outlet is yellow, matching the standard colour code for reduced low-voltage site equipment. Blue is used for 230V supplies, so the distinct colours stop tools being plugged into the wrong, more dangerous voltage.

A.text: Black is not the BS EN 60309 identification colour for a 110 V reduced-low-voltage site connector.

B.text: Blue identifies the normal 200-250 V range, so it distinguishes 230 V equipment from the site 110 V supply.

C.text: Red identifies the 380-480 V range, commonly used for 400 V three-phase connections rather than 110 V.

D.text: The 110V outlet is yellow, matching the standard colour code for reduced low-voltage site equipment. Blue is used for 230V supplies, so the distinct colours stop tools being plugged into the wrong, more dangerous voltage.

questions.prompt: Where there is no local means of isolation for equipment or circuits to be worked on, which of the following is the preferred method of isolation?

options.A: Disconnecting the individual circuit from the DB
options.B: Isolation of the individual circuit breaker or fuse
options.C: Isolation of the main switch or DB switch- disconnector
options.D: Pulling out the distributor's cut-out fuse

questions.explanation: Without a local isolator, you isolate at the main switch or board switch-disconnector, which is designed to safely break the supply on load and can be locked off. Pulling the supplier's cut-out fuse is not yours to touch, and unbolting a circuit live is unsafe.

A.text: Disconnecting conductors at the board is more intrusive and unnecessary where the board's main isolator can secure all supplies.

B.text: The premise states there is no local circuit isolation, so relying on an individual breaker or fuse does not solve it.

C.text: Without a local isolator, you isolate at the main switch or board switch-disconnector, which is designed to safely break the supply on load and can be locked off. Pulling the supplier's cut-out fuse is not yours to touch, and unbolting a circuit live is unsafe.

D.text: The distributor's sealed cut-out is not for ordinary contractors to remove and may expose dangerous live parts.

questions.prompt: What action should you take if a workmate gets an electric shock?

options.A: Cut off the power and call for help
options.B: Dial 999 and ask for the fire brigade
options.D: Try to pull them to safety

questions.explanation: If you can switch the power off, the electric hazard will be removed. First aid assistance will then probably be required. Do not touch someone who is still in contact with live electrical cables as you could also receive an electric shock.

A.text: If you can switch the power off, the electric hazard will be removed. First aid assistance will then probably be required. Do not touch someone who is still in contact with live electrical cables as you could also receive an electric shock.

B.text: Emergency medical help may be needed, but asking specifically for the fire brigade does not first stop current through the casualty.

C.text: The network operator is not the immediate rescue service and a phone call leaves the casualty connected to danger.

D.text: Touching or pulling the casualty before isolation can pass the shock current through the rescuer too.

questions.prompt: A residual current device is designed to operate in the event of one of the following:
questions.explanation: An RCD detects an imbalance between line and neutral currents, which occurs when current leaks to earth, and trips quickly to protect against electric shock. Overloads and short-circuits are handled by fuses or MCBs, not the RCD.

A.text: An RCD detects an imbalance between line and neutral currents, which occurs when current leaks to earth, and trips quickly to protect against electric shock. Overloads and short-circuits are handled by fuses or MCBs, not the RCD.

B.text: A lightning surge may create several effects, but an RCD is not specifically a lightning-protection device.

C.text: Overload protection is provided by a fuse or overcurrent circuit-breaker; balanced load current does not trip an RCD.

D.text: A line-neutral short circuit is an overcurrent fault with balanced outgoing and returning current, so an RCD alone may not respond.

questions.prompt: Electrical installations on construction sites should be periodically inspected and tested:
questions.explanation: Three monthly inspections of construction site installations are recommended in IEE Guidance Note 3.

A.text: Three monthly inspections of construction site installations are recommended in IEE Guidance Note 3.

B.text: Six months exceeds the commonly specified three-month construction-site interval for temporary installations.

C.text: Monthly inspection may be chosen for higher risk, but it is not the stated general periodic interval.

D.text: A yearly interval is too long for temporary systems exposed to frequent movement, weather and site damage.

questions.prompt: Which listed value is the conventional upper boundary of extra-low voltage for AC and the level above which HSE warns that contact can cause shock injury?
questions.explanation: Fifty volts AC is a conventional voltage boundary used in electrical-safety measures; it is not a guaranteed safe body-withstand voltage. Shock outcome also depends on current path, duration, skin condition, environment and other factors, and HSE warns that contact above about 50 V AC can injure.

A.text: One hundred and ten volts exceeds the conventional extra-low-voltage boundary even when centre-tapped site supplies reduce voltage to earth.

B.text: Two hundred and thirty volts is ordinary single-phase low voltage and presents a substantial contact-shock hazard.

C.text: Four hundred volts is a three-phase low-voltage system value and is far above the extra-low-voltage boundary.

D.text: Fifty volts AC is a conventional voltage boundary used in electrical-safety measures; it is not a guaranteed safe body-withstand voltage. Shock outcome also depends on current path, duration, skin condition, environment and other factors, and HSE warns that contact above about 50 V AC can injure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true with regard to the dangers of electricity?

options.A: Electricity is dangerous at any time because you cannot tell by looking at a cable whether or not it is live
options.B: Electricity is only dangerous if you are not wearing wellington boots
options.C: Electricity is only dangerous in wet weather
options.D: Electricity is perfectly safe so long as you wear cotton gloves

questions.explanation: The features which make electricity so dangerous are that you cannot see, hear or smell it. It can give you a very unpleasant surprise. Always assume that cables are live.

A.text: The features which make electricity so dangerous are that you cannot see, hear or smell it. It can give you a very unpleasant surprise. Always assume that cables are live.

B.text: Wellington boots are not a universal electrical safeguard and may be wet, damaged or unsuitable for the voltage.

C.text: Dry weather does not prove a conductor dead or remove the possibility of a fatal current path.

D.text: Cotton gloves have no electrical insulating rating and do not make contact with energised parts safe.

questions.prompt: What is the most serious effect that electric shock can have if you come into contact with a live part?

options.A: The electric current can cause a slight tingling in the fingers
options.B: The electric current can cause burn marks on the fingers
options.C: The electric current can cause the finger muscles to twitch
options.D: The electric current can cause the heart to stop, resulting in death

questions.explanation: Contact with live electrical parts can be fatal. If you do not know otherwise, always assume that electrical parts are live.

A.text: Tingling is an early shock effect, but it is less severe than a current path that stops the heart.

B.text: Burns can be serious and deep, yet cardiac arrest presents the more immediate fatal consequence listed.

C.text: Muscle twitching shows physiological stimulation, but it is not the most severe outcome among these choices.

D.text: Contact with live electrical parts can be fatal. If you do not know otherwise, always assume that electrical parts are live.

questions.prompt: Your job involves you working near to hanging electrical cables which have bare ends. What should you do?

options.A: Attempt to push the cables back into the ceiling void so that you can start work
options.B: Carry on working, as there shouldn't be a problem
options.C: Inform your supervisor and keep well away
options.D: Touch the cables to see if they are live

questions.explanation: You must always assume that exposed cables are live until you know they are not. Contact with live electrical cables can kill.

A.text: Moving unidentified bare conductors may bring them into contact with the worker or another live surface.

B.text: Appearance cannot prove the ends dead, so continuing nearby leaves an uncontrolled electrocution and arc risk.

C.text: You must always assume that exposed cables are live until you know they are not. Contact with live electrical cables can kill.

D.text: The human body must never be used as a voltage detector; touching can produce fatal current before any reaction is possible.

questions.prompt: For all live working activities it is necessary to:

options.B: Carry out a risk assessment as required by the EAW Regulations.

questions.explanation: Live work is only justified when unavoidable, and the Electricity at Work Regulations require a risk assessment to confirm it is reasonable and to set the precautions needed. This drives the decision on accompaniment, PPE and any other controls.

A.text: A second person may form part of precautions, but accompaniment is not the universal legal basis for every live task.

B.text: Live work is only justified when unavoidable, and the Electricity at Work Regulations require a risk assessment to confirm it is reasonable and to set the precautions needed. This drives the decision on accompaniment, PPE and any other controls.

C.text: Chance and optimism are not controls and provide no evidence that live work has been justified or made safe.

D.text: Gloves alone cannot control arcing, inadvertent contact, unsuitable tools or the need to avoid live work.

questions.prompt: An electrical Permit to Work is primarily a statement that:

options.A: Certain instructions need to be followed
options.B: Someone else has taken responsibility for the work
options.C: The circuit or equipment has been isolated and is safe to work on
options.D: The circuit or equipment is live

questions.explanation: Permits to work describe the procedures that prevent a major hazard, such as electricity or moving machinery, from causing harm, usually by isolation to effectively ensure (in the case of electricity) 'dead' working with no chance of it going 'live'.

A.text: A permit contains instructions, but its central assurance is the defined equipment state and boundary released for work.

B.text: Issuing a permit coordinates responsibilities; it does not transfer all responsibility away from the people doing the work.

C.text: Permits to work describe the procedures that prevent a major hazard, such as electricity or moving machinery, from causing harm, usually by isolation to effectively ensure (in the case of electricity) 'dead' working with no chance of it going 'live'.

D.text: A permit-to-work for dead work is not authority to treat the circuit as live or to bypass isolation.

questions.prompt: The probes of voltage detectors and test instruments used on electrical systems should be:

options.D: Shaped or have barriers to prevent finger contact with the tips

questions.explanation: In addition, to protect against damage by overcurrent whilst in use, the probes or instrument should incorporate suitable high breaking capacity (hbc) fuses with a low current rating (usually not exceeding 500 mA), or current-limiting resistors.

A.text: Calibration evidence concerns instrument accuracy; it does not stop a finger sliding onto an exposed probe tip.

B.text: Colour can help identification but provides no physical protection against touching conductive metal.

C.text: Country of manufacture does not determine probe safety; construction, ratings and exposed-tip protection do.

D.text: In addition, to protect against damage by overcurrent whilst in use, the probes or instrument should incorporate suitable high breaking capacity (hbc) fuses with a low current rating (usually not exceeding 500 mA), or current-limiting resistors.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does the Electricity at Work (EAW) regulations apply to?

options.A: All persons engaged for work purposes

questions.explanation: The EAW Regulations impose duties on employers, employees and the self employed.

A.text: The EAW Regulations impose duties on employers, employees and the self employed.

B.text: The Regulations also impose duties beyond employees, including on employers and self-employed people at work.

C.text: Employers carry major duties, but employees and self-employed people also have obligations under the Regulations.

D.text: Self-employed people are covered, but limiting the scope to them excludes employees and employers who are also covered.

questions.prompt: In accordance with the Electricity at Work regulations, when considering whether to work live a responsible person should:
questions.explanation: To identify and assess the risks involved and the methods of controlling them.

A.text: To identify and assess the risks involved and the methods of controlling them.

B.text: A client's demand cannot displace the legal duty to assess and control the danger created by live work.

C.text: Dead working is the normal approach, but the decision process still requires assessment of the actual circumstances.

D.text: Live work is exceptional, not an automatic method to choose without first evaluating whether it is justified.

questions.prompt: The normal procedure for working on electrical equipment should be which one of the following?
questions.explanation: Dead working should be considered as the norm and work on or near live conductors should rarely be permitted

A.text: Dead working should be considered as the norm and work on or near live conductors should rarely be permitted

B.text: Live working is exceptional and must satisfy strict legal conditions; it is not the normal procedure.

C.text: Insulated tools are a supplementary precaution and do not justify leaving equipment energised unnecessarily.

D.text: Insulating gloves cannot replace secure isolation and proof of dead before ordinary electrical work.

questions.prompt: Test instruments used for working on electrical systems should:
questions.explanation: To protect the user from electric shock whilst using the instrument, i.e. handling the probes.

A.text: Age does not demonstrate electrical condition or suitability; instruments require appropriate design, maintenance and checks.

B.text: Yellow colour has no protective function and cannot establish voltage rating or finger-safe construction.

C.text: To protect the user from electric shock whilst using the instrument, i.e. handling the probes.

D.text: Bare probes increase the chance of bridging conductors or touching live metal and conflict with safe test-lead guidance.

questions.prompt: Under the Electricity at Work Regulations, live working is considered:

options.C: Only to be allowed in exceptional circumstances

questions.explanation: Extra controls must be employed, including training, supervision and use of suitable tools and protective equipment.

A.text: Live work is not freely acceptable; each task must satisfy the strict conditions in Regulation 14.

B.text: An absolute ban is also inaccurate because carefully justified live work is lawful in exceptional circumstances.

C.text: Extra controls must be employed, including training, supervision and use of suitable tools and protective equipment.

D.text: Normalising live work reverses the hierarchy: equipment should ordinarily be isolated and proved dead.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would you use to replace the fuse in a plug if fuses were NOT available?
questions.explanation: A fuse is often the main safety device in an electrical circuit. A blown fuse must only be replaced by a fuse of the correct type and rating.

A.text: A wire link has unknown current characteristics and can allow the flex or appliance to overheat and catch fire.

B.text: A nail will not melt safely under fault current and can leave the plug and cable without overcurrent protection.

C.text: Silver paper can bridge the fuse clips indefinitely, creating overheating and shock risk instead of controlled disconnection.

D.text: A fuse is often the main safety device in an electrical circuit. A blown fuse must only be replaced by a fuse of the correct type and rating.

questions.prompt: To prove a circuit or equipment is dead after isolation what is the FIRST activity in the sequence of events?

options.C: Check that the voltage detector is working on a proving device, known live source or in- built test feature
options.D: Make sure equipment is not working

questions.explanation: This will prove that that the voltage detector (such as a two-pole voltage detector or proprietary test lamp) is working, i.e. indicating voltage.

A.text: Testing line to earth is part of proving dead, but the detector must first be proved functional.

B.text: A line-neutral test can falsely reassure if the detector has failed; pre-use proving must precede circuit measurements.

C.text: This will prove that that the voltage detector (such as a two-pole voltage detector or proprietary test lamp) is working, i.e. indicating voltage.

D.text: Equipment not operating may result from a control fault and does not prove every conductor is dead.

questions.prompt: The nominal single phase voltage in the UK is?
questions.explanation: This is the nominal voltage for public electricity supply systems within Europe.

A.text: This is the nominal voltage for public electricity supply systems within Europe.

B.text: The harmonised UK nominal single-phase supply is 230 V, even though measured voltage may be near the historical 240 V value.

C.text: Four hundred volts is the nominal voltage between phases on a three-phase system, not single phase to neutral.

D.text: Four hundred and fifteen volts is the former three-phase nominal value and is not the present single-phase rating.

questions.prompt: Under Regulation 14 of the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989, when may work on or near a live conductor that may give rise to danger proceed?

options.A: Only when it is unreasonable in all the circumstances for the conductor to be dead, it is reasonable to work live, and suitable precautions are taken to prevent injury
options.B: When the means of isolation cannot be identified
options.C: When the person carrying out the work is a competent person
options.D: When the person working on the equipment is wearing rubber gloves

questions.explanation: All three Regulation 14 conditions must be satisfied. Live work must be justified because making dead is unreasonable, carrying it out live must itself be reasonable, and suitable precautions, including suitable protective equipment where necessary, must prevent injury.

A.text: All three Regulation 14 conditions must be satisfied. Live work must be justified because making dead is unreasonable, carrying it out live must itself be reasonable, and suitable precautions, including suitable protective equipment where necessary, must prevent injury.

B.text: Difficulty identifying isolation does not satisfy the statutory tests; the supply must be traced and the work properly planned.

C.text: Competence is necessary for dangerous electrical work, but competence alone does not justify leaving the conductor live.

D.text: Rubber gloves are only one possible precaution and cannot replace the three legal conditions for live work.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a requirement of low voltage safe isolation practice?

options.A: A caution notice should be applied at the point of isolation
options.B: Ensuring that the correct point of isolation is identified
options.C: The conductors are proved to be dead at the point of work
options.D: The person carrying out the work is issued with insulating gloves

questions.explanation: Safe isolation practice refers to dead working. The use of insulating gloves will generally only be applicable to live working.

A.text: A caution notice communicates the isolation and warns others not to operate the secured device.

B.text: Identifying the correct isolator prevents the wrong circuit being locked while the intended conductors remain live.

C.text: Proving dead at the work point confirms isolation has actually removed dangerous voltage from every relevant conductor.

D.text: Safe isolation practice refers to dead working. The use of insulating gloves will generally only be applicable to live working.

questions.prompt: The specific effects on the human body of a major electric shock are one of the following:
questions.explanation: A major electric shock drives current through the body, causing deep burns where it enters and exits and disrupting the heart's rhythm, leading to cardiac arrest. These are the immediate life-threatening effects, unlike chest pains or dermatitis.

A.text: Broken bones can follow a fall caused by shock, but they are not the characteristic direct electrical effects listed.

B.text: A major electric shock drives current through the body, causing deep burns where it enters and exits and disrupting the heart's rhythm, leading to cardiac arrest. These are the immediate life-threatening effects, unlike chest pains or dermatitis.

C.text: Chest pain can occur, yet the major direct outcomes include severe burns and disruption of the heart rhythm.

D.text: Dermatitis is skin inflammation from irritants or allergy, not an acute effect of a major electric current path.

questions.prompt: The lowest level of electrical current which can harm the human body is normally measured in:
questions.explanation: Research has shown that a person is in serious danger of a fatal electric shock at, or above, approximately 30 milliamps.

A.text: Whole amperes are far above the range where shock can already disrupt breathing or heart rhythm.

B.text: Kiloamperes describe fault-current magnitudes, not the small body current capable of causing physiological injury.

C.text: Microamperes are one-thousandth of a milliampere and are generally below the ordinary harmful-shock thresholds discussed.

D.text: Research has shown that a person is in serious danger of a fatal electric shock at, or above, approximately 30 milliamps.

questions.prompt: Which listed device is specifically intended to provide additional protection against electric shock by rapidly disconnecting for some residual-current faults?

options.A: A 3 amp fuse should prevent a person receiving a fatal electric shock
options.B: A 30 mA Residual Current Device (RCD), although it does not make contact with live parts safe or guarantee survival
options.C: A 5 amp rewireable fuse should prevent a person receiving a fatal electric shock
options.D: A 6 amp circuit breaker should prevent a person receiving a fatal electric shock

questions.explanation: A 30 mA RCD can limit the energy in some electric shocks and can save life, but it detects only residual-current imbalance and is additional protection. It cannot replace isolation, earthing, basic protection or safe working practice, and it does not guarantee that a shock will not be fatal.

A.text: A 3 A fuse protects wiring against sustained overcurrent; it may carry far more than a lethal body current without operating.

B.text: A 30 mA RCD can limit the energy in some electric shocks and can save life, but it detects only residual-current imbalance and is additional protection. It cannot replace isolation, earthing, basic protection or safe working practice, and it does not guarantee that a shock will not be fatal.

C.text: A rewireable fuse responds to circuit overcurrent, not the small residual imbalance associated with a person receiving a shock.

D.text: A 6 A breaker is intended for overload and short-circuit protection and is not sensitive enough for personal shock protection.

questions.prompt: Where mains voltage is used to supply portable equipment on a construction site, what additional protection is required?
questions.explanation: Reduced low voltage systems (e.g. 110 volt centre point earthed) are strongly preferred in such circumstances. Where only mains voltage (230 V) equipment is available, however, a 30 mA RCD will give additional protection against fatal electric shock.

A.text: A cable locator prevents excavation strikes and provides no automatic disconnection for a shock from portable equipment.

B.text: Reduced low voltage systems (e.g. 110 volt centre point earthed) are strongly preferred in such circumstances. Where only mains voltage (230 V) equipment is available, however, a 30 mA RCD will give additional protection against fatal electric shock.

C.text: A generator is a source, not additional personal shock protection for a 230 V portable appliance.

D.text: A step-down transformer would change the equipment voltage and cannot supply a tool designed solely for 230 V at its rated operation.

questions.prompt: A mobile plant operator can let you ride in the machine:

options.B: If it is designed to carry passengers
options.D: If you have a long way to go

questions.explanation: You may only ride in mobile plant if it is purpose-built with a proper seat and restraint for a passenger. Riding on machines not designed to carry people, such as on forks or buckets, risks being thrown off or crushed.

A.text: Plant must never carry people on steps, buckets or other undesigned positions merely because the operator agrees.

B.text: You may only ride in mobile plant if it is purpose-built with a proper seat and restraint for a passenger. Riding on machines not designed to carry people, such as on forks or buckets, risks being thrown off or crushed.

C.text: Rain increases slip and visibility hazards and does not create an exception to passenger-design requirements.

D.text: Journey length cannot justify riding on machinery that lacks a designated seat and restraint.

questions.prompt: What must be considered first when planning to carry out work in a confined space?

options.A: Can the work be done from the outside
options.C: Has the job been priced properly
options.D: Have the correct tools been arranged

questions.explanation: Working outside will remove the risks of working in the confined space.

A.text: Working outside will remove the risks of working in the confined space.

B.text: Staffing is considered only after establishing that entry is unavoidable and assessing the confined-space hazards.

C.text: Commercial pricing cannot determine whether a worker should be exposed to a dangerous enclosed atmosphere.

D.text: Tool selection follows the safe method; arranging tools first assumes entry before avoidance has been considered.

questions.prompt: When working in a confined space, such as a sewer, what danger may occur?

options.D: Not enough time for the job to be done

questions.explanation: Confined spaces like sewers can accumulate toxic, flammable or oxygen-displacing gases that you cannot always see or smell, so air must be tested before entry. Boredom and time pressure are inconveniences, not the life-threatening danger here.

A.text: Boredom is not the specified serious confined-space hazard and does not explain rapid incapacitation in a sewer.

B.text: Confined spaces like sewers can accumulate toxic, flammable or oxygen-displacing gases that you cannot always see or smell, so air must be tested before entry. Boredom and time pressure are inconveniences, not the life-threatening danger here.

C.text: Getting wet is uncomfortable and can add electrical risk, but harmful atmosphere is the central sewer danger listed.

D.text: Time pressure affects planning but is not an inherent atmospheric hazard created by the confined space.

questions.prompt: To determine the safety of the atmosphere in an excavation, which of the following is essential

options.B: Only entering for a short period to enable a quick escape

questions.explanation: Use a suitable detector. Many dangerous gases have no smell, and cannot be seen. Workers can be overcome in seconds in dangerous atmospheres.

A.text: Toxic gases and oxygen deficiency are often invisible, so visual inspection cannot establish atmospheric safety.

B.text: A dangerous atmosphere can overcome a worker before a quick escape is possible, even during a short entry.

C.text: Smell is unreliable and the attempt exposes the worker; some lethal gases have no detectable odour.

D.text: Use a suitable detector. Many dangerous gases have no smell, and cannot be seen. Workers can be overcome in seconds in dangerous atmospheres.

questions.prompt: Before entering an excavation to start work, it must first be:
questions.explanation: Excavation work is hazardous. A competent person, knowledgeable about how to reduce risks, notably from collapse of the walls, must inspect the excavation first.

A.text: Covering and waiting does not establish that the sides, access, atmosphere or buried services are safe.

B.text: Flooding an excavation adds instability and drowning risk and is not a substitute for competent inspection.

C.text: Excavation work is hazardous. A competent person, knowledgeable about how to reduce risks, notably from collapse of the walls, must inspect the excavation first.

D.text: The duty is for a competent appointed person to inspect; an HSE inspector does not approve each excavation before entry.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of using a 'permit to work' system?

options.A: To enable tools and equipment to be properly checked before the commencement of work
options.B: To ensure that the client will pay for the work
options.C: To ensure the job is carried out by the quickest method
options.D: To help ensure a safe system of work

questions.explanation: A permit to work is a written system used to control certain types of hazardous work. They allow work to start only when site procedures have been clarified.

A.text: Tool checks may be included, but a permit principally coordinates hazards, isolations, boundaries and authorisation for the work.

B.text: Payment belongs to the contract and is unrelated to the permit's control of hazardous work.

C.text: Speed is not the permit's objective and can conflict with the deliberate checks required for safe execution.

D.text: A permit to work is a written system used to control certain types of hazardous work. They allow work to start only when site procedures have been clarified.

questions.prompt: Why may young people be more at risk on site?

options.A: There is no requirement to provide PPE to young people
options.B: There is no specific legislation applying to them
options.C: They are inexperienced and may not recognize danger
options.D: They are usually left to work alone to gain experience

questions.explanation: Health and Safety guidance lists young people as often being 'at particular risk', due to their lack of practical experience.

A.text: Young workers have the same right to suitable PPE where risk remains; age does not remove the employer's duty.

B.text: Health and safety law includes specific protection for young people through assessment of their inexperience and maturity.

C.text: Health and Safety guidance lists young people as often being 'at particular risk', due to their lack of practical experience.

D.text: Leaving an inexperienced person alone would increase rather than explain or control their vulnerability.

questions.prompt: You have to enter a manhole in which you know there are toxic gases. You have all the PPE but there does not appear to be a rescue plan in place. What should you do?

options.A: Ask your mate to stand-by at the top of the manhole with a length of rope
options.B: Do not enter the manhole until a rescue plan and rescue equipment are in place
options.C: Just get on and do the job, it will probably be alright
options.D: Plan to carry out the job in short bursts

questions.explanation: A rescue plan must be in place before anyone enters a confined space. This is one of the requirements of the Confined Spaces Regulations 1997.

A.text: A person with a rope is not a competent rescue system and may become another casualty without suitable equipment.

B.text: A rescue plan must be in place before anyone enters a confined space. This is one of the requirements of the Confined Spaces Regulations 1997.

C.text: Possessing PPE does not control foreseeable emergency recovery, so entry without a rescue plan remains unsafe.

D.text: Short entries can still lead to sudden incapacitation, and planned bursts do not provide rescue capability.

questions.prompt: You are asked to enter a manhole where a toxic or oxygen-deficient atmosphere may be present, but no assessed safe system or suitable respiratory protection has been provided. What should you do?

options.A: Just get on with the job, and accept the risks
options.B: Look into the manhole to see if you can see any harmful gases
options.C: Sniff the atmosphere in the manhole to see if you can smell harmful gases
options.D: Do not enter; report it so entry can be avoided or a competent risk-assessed system, atmosphere controls, training and rescue arrangements can be put in place

questions.explanation: Confined-space entry should be avoided where possible. If it is essential, the employer must assess the atmosphere and other risks, implement a safe system, provide suitable equipment and training, and establish adequate rescue arrangements before entry. Asking only for generic RPE would be incomplete.

A.text: Entering without controls risks rapid collapse, poisoning or asphyxiation and may also endanger would-be rescuers.

B.text: Many toxic gases and oxygen deficiency are invisible, so looking into the opening cannot establish a safe atmosphere.

C.text: Hazardous atmospheres may have no warning odour, and sniffing exposes the worker before any measurement is made.

D.text: Confined-space entry should be avoided where possible. If it is essential, the employer must assess the atmosphere and other risks, implement a safe system, provide suitable equipment and training, and establish adequate rescue arrangements before entry. Asking only for generic RPE would be incomplete.

questions.prompt: While digging a trench, you uncover a length of yellow marker tape at a depth of about 150mm. What does the presence of the marker tape mean?

options.A: The area has a high water-table and precautions must be taken to prevent an in-rush of water
options.B: The excavation has reached a depth where the sides must now be supported
options.C: There is a buried electrical cable and further excavation must be carried out with care
options.D: There is contaminated soil below the level of the marker tape and all excavation must stop

questions.explanation: The coloured tape indicates that there are buried services below the route of the tape.

A.text: Electrical warning tape identifies a service route, not groundwater conditions or a need to dewater the excavation.

B.text: Support requirements depend on ground and excavation risk, not on the colour of buried service marker tape.

C.text: The coloured tape indicates that there are buried services below the route of the tape.

D.text: Contaminated land requires separate evidence and controls; yellow service tape is not a soil-contamination marker.

questions.prompt: A Cable Avoidance Tool (C.A.T.) and a 'Genny' (generator) can be used successfully to locate underground cables by whom:
questions.explanation: Equipment used to locate buried services must only be used by people who have been trained to use it.

A.text: Equipment used to locate buried services must only be used by people who have been trained to use it.

B.text: Employment by an electricity company does not prove training on the particular locator or site conditions.

C.text: Incorrect CAT and Genny use can falsely show an area clear, so unrestricted use by anyone is unsafe.

D.text: A foreman's role does not automatically include locator competence; training and demonstrated skill remain necessary.

questions.prompt: After plans and a suitable locating device have identified an underground power cable, which listed approach should be used for trial holes and final exposure?

options.A: A 360 degree excavator with rubber tyres
options.D: Careful safe digging with suitable hand tools, using insulated tools near the cable and exposing it from the side where practicable

questions.explanation: HSE requires planning, cable plans, trained use of locating devices and safe excavation. Trial holes and final exposure normally use carefully controlled suitable hand tools, with insulated tools near electricity cables; 'hand digging' alone was too vague to describe the safe system.

A.text: Rubber tyres do not prevent a bucket tooth cutting a live cable or protect people from arc-flash energy.

B.text: A powered breaker can penetrate cable protection before the operator detects it and is unsuitable for final exposure.

C.text: A pickaxe concentrates uncontrolled impact at its point and can pierce a cable with little warning.

D.text: HSE requires planning, cable plans, trained use of locating devices and safe excavation. Trial holes and final exposure normally use carefully controlled suitable hand tools, with insulated tools near electricity cables; 'hand digging' alone was too vague to describe the safe system.

questions.prompt: When do special precautions need to be taken when working near overhead electric power lines?

options.A: Only if cranes etc. are being used
options.B: Only if plant has to pass under the lines
options.C: Only if someone could touch a line with their bare hands
options.D: Whenever work areas will be near or beneath the lines

questions.explanation: Actual contact with a power line is not necessary to result in an electric shock as a close approach may allow 'flashover' to occur. HSE publication GS6 gives advice on procedures to avoid such danger.

A.text: Cranes are one concern, but ladders, scaffold tubes, tipping bodies and MEWPs can also reach overhead conductors.

B.text: People, loads and equipment can approach a line even without passing directly underneath it.

C.text: Electricity can arc across an air gap, so bare-hand contact is not required for serious injury.

D.text: Actual contact with a power line is not necessary to result in an electric shock as a close approach may allow 'flashover' to occur. HSE publication GS6 gives advice on procedures to avoid such danger.

questions.prompt: When working alone:

options.A: Don't bother anyone if you have a problem, always sort it out yourself
options.B: Make sure someone responsible knows where you are
options.C: Wear headphones, it will make the day go more quickly
options.D: You can do away with protective equipment

questions.explanation: Employees should adhere to safe working arrangements put in place by their employer. When working alone, such arrangements should include informing a responsible person of your location periodically.

A.text: Lone-working arrangements must provide a way to obtain assistance; self-reliance cannot control emergencies or incapacitation.

B.text: Employees should adhere to safe working arrangements put in place by their employer. When working alone, such arrangements should include informing a responsible person of your location periodically.

C.text: Headphones can mask alarms, vehicles and calls for help, increasing isolation rather than managing it.

D.text: Working alone does not remove any hazard, so the assessed protective equipment remains necessary.

questions.prompt: You have to walk across a site several times a day, but have to dodge a lot of site traffic. The first thing you should do is:

options.B: Jump on the back of a vehicle if you can, it's safer than walking
options.C: Tell your supervisor about the danger
options.D: Walk around the edges of the site to keep out of the way

questions.explanation: Pedestrian routes should have been set up to keep people and vehicles apart, so inform your employer if the system is not working. Don't hitch rides on vehicles unless safe seating is provided.

A.text: Speaking informally to drivers does not redesign the route or place the traffic risk under site management control.

B.text: Riding on an undesigned part of a vehicle creates a crushing or fall risk and is not a safe alternative to walking.

C.text: Pedestrian routes should have been set up to keep people and vehicles apart, so inform your employer if the system is not working. Don't hitch rides on vehicles unless safe seating is provided.

D.text: Walking at the edge may introduce blind corners or reversing hazards and should not replace an assessed pedestrian route.

questions.prompt: Why may a confined space be dangerous to work in?

options.A: Air in the space may be unbreathable due to poisonous gas
options.C: Temperature and poor ventilation may affect the worker
options.D: There may not be sufficient working space

questions.explanation: There can be a range of hazards associated with confined spaces, and these can include all of those mentioned

A.text: A poisonous or oxygen-deficient atmosphere is one confined-space hazard, but heat, access and restricted movement also matter.

B.text: There can be a range of hazards associated with confined spaces, and these can include all of those mentioned

C.text: Temperature and ventilation are important, but this choice omits atmospheric toxicity and restricted working space.

D.text: Restricted space can hamper work and rescue, but it does not capture the separate atmospheric and thermal dangers.

questions.prompt: What action should you take if an electric drill cuts out while you are using it?

options.A: Put it back into the tool box
options.B: Remove it from use and tell your supervisor
options.D: Switch the power off and on

questions.prompt: A person nearly collapses complaining of stomach pains. What should you do?
