options.B: Go and find them something to drink
options.C: Help them to find somewhere comfortable to sit

questions.explanation: Near-collapse with abdominal pain can signal a serious internal problem, so get the trained first-aider immediately. Giving food or drink could be dangerous if the casualty later needs surgery or worsens.

A.text: Food can complicate urgent treatment and does not obtain a trained assessment for a person close to collapse.

B.text: Giving a drink may be unsafe if surgery or reduced consciousness follows, and it delays summoning competent help.

C.text: A comfortable seat may prevent a fall, but it does not address the unexplained pain and near-collapse medically.

D.text: Near-collapse with abdominal pain can signal a serious internal problem, so get the trained first-aider immediately. Giving food or drink could be dangerous if the casualty later needs surgery or worsens.

questions.prompt: A workmate lifting a big box suddenly shouts "oh, my back" and drops the box. What should you do?

options.A: Find them somewhere comfortable to sit and rest
options.B: Help them to lift the box
options.D: Tell them to leave it for someone else to lift

questions.explanation: The priority for any back injury is to obtain first-aid advice, in order to prevent further damage.

A.text: Rest may feel helpful, but sudden back pain after lifting needs assessment before the casualty is moved or work resumes.

B.text: Continuing the lift can worsen the casualty's injury and expose the helper to the same uncontrolled load.

C.text: The priority for any back injury is to obtain first-aid advice, in order to prevent further damage.

D.text: Leaving the box addresses the task but not the injured person, who still needs competent first-aid assessment.

questions.prompt: Modern portable fire extinguishers are predominantly red. How is the extinguishing medium additionally identified?

options.A: By the extinguisher's wording and a permitted colour-coded panel or band on the red body
options.B: During site induction, you will be told where the different types of extinguishers are
options.C: The type of extinguisher is written on a sign next to it
options.D: The weight and shape of the extinguisher

questions.explanation: The extinguisher label names the medium and a limited colour-coded area helps rapid identification, while the body is predominantly red. Location and shape alone are not reliable ways to choose the correct extinguisher for a fire.

A.text: The extinguisher label names the medium and a limited colour-coded area helps rapid identification, while the body is predominantly red. Location and shape alone are not reliable ways to choose the correct extinguisher for a fire.

B.text: Induction may explain locations, but memory of location does not identify an unfamiliar extinguisher in an emergency.

C.text: A nearby wall sign can be missing or obscured; identification must be carried on the extinguisher itself.

D.text: Different media can use similar cylinders, so weight and shape are not the standard identification system.

questions.prompt: A black-labelled fire extinguisher contains:
questions.explanation: A black label denotes a carbon dioxide (CO2) extinguisher, suited to electrical and flammable-liquid fires because it smothers the flames with gas and leaves no residue to damage equipment.

A.text: A black label denotes a carbon dioxide (CO2) extinguisher, suited to electrical and flammable-liquid fires because it smothers the flames with gas and leaves no residue to damage equipment.

B.text: Dry powder uses the blue identification panel, not the black panel associated with carbon dioxide.

C.text: Foam is identified by a cream panel and has different suitability from carbon dioxide on electrical equipment.

D.text: A water extinguisher is all red or carries the water wording, rather than a black medium panel.

questions.prompt: What is a blue-labelled fire extinguisher filled with?
questions.explanation: A blue label identifies a dry powder extinguisher, a versatile type that knocks down liquid, gas and electrical fires by interrupting the chemical reaction of combustion.

A.text: Carbon dioxide is identified by black, not blue, and discharges as a gas rather than powder.

B.text: A blue label identifies a dry powder extinguisher, a versatile type that knocks down liquid, gas and electrical fires by interrupting the chemical reaction of combustion.

C.text: Foam carries a cream identification panel and is selected for different classes of fire.

D.text: Water is identified by the plain red scheme and must not be confused with blue-labelled powder.

questions.prompt: Which fire extinguisher should not be used on flammable liquid fires?
questions.explanation: Water must never be used on flammable liquid fires because the burning fuel floats on the water and spreads, while the jet can splash the liquid and rapidly enlarge the fire.

A.text: Carbon dioxide can smother a small flammable-liquid fire without spreading the burning liquid across the floor.

B.text: Suitable foam forms a blanket over many flammable liquids and suppresses vapour when used for its rated fire class.

C.text: Dry powder interrupts combustion and is rated for flammable-liquid fires, although its discharge has visibility drawbacks.

D.text: Water must never be used on flammable liquid fires because the burning fuel floats on the water and spreads, while the jet can splash the liquid and rapidly enlarge the fire.

questions.prompt: What colour is a water filled fire extinguisher, or its label?
questions.explanation: Water extinguishers carry an all-red body with a red label. Under the colour-coding scheme red is the base signal colour, and water is the default type that bears no additional coloured panel.

A.text: Black identifies carbon dioxide, a gas used for different fire risks from ordinary water extinguishers.

B.text: Cream identifies foam, not water, despite both media being useful on some solid combustibles.

C.text: Green is not the current UK identification colour for a water extinguisher.

D.text: Water extinguishers carry an all-red body with a red label. Under the colour-coding scheme red is the base signal colour, and water is the default type that bears no additional coloured panel.

questions.prompt: When discharging carbon dioxide fire extinguishers, the nozzle:
questions.explanation: The expansion of CO2 gas coming out of the nozzle causes rapid cooling.

A.text: The expansion of CO2 gas coming out of the nozzle causes rapid cooling.

B.text: Rapid expansion of carbon dioxide absorbs heat; it does not heat the discharge horn.

C.text: The horn can become cold enough to cause a freeze burn, so describing it as merely warm is unsafe.

D.text: Its temperature changes sharply during discharge because the expanding gas cools the horn.

questions.prompt: For fires involving spilled petrol, which types of fire extinguisher could you use?

options.A: Foam, carbon dioxide or dry powder
options.B: Water, carbon dioxide or dry powder

questions.explanation: Spilled petrol is a flammable liquid (Class B) fire. Foam blankets and seals the surface, while CO2 and dry powder smother the flames. Water is unsafe as it spreads the burning fuel.

A.text: Spilled petrol is a flammable liquid (Class B) fire. Foam blankets and seals the surface, while CO2 and dry powder smother the flames. Water is unsafe as it spreads the burning fuel.

B.text: This combination includes water, which can spread floating petrol and enlarge the burning surface.

C.text: Carbon dioxide and foam may be suitable, but adding water makes the listed combination unsafe for spilled petrol.

D.text: Powder and foam may control the fire, yet the water in this group can carry burning fuel outward.

questions.prompt: Which types of fire extinguishers should be used on electrical fires?
questions.explanation: CO2 and dry powder are non-conductive, so they will not carry current back to the user. Foam and water conduct electricity and risk electric shock, making them unsafe on live electrical fires.

A.text: CO2 and dry powder are non-conductive, so they will not carry current back to the user. Foam and water conduct electricity and risk electric shock, making them unsafe on live electrical fires.

B.text: Dry powder can be used, but ordinary foam is conductive or leaves residue and is not the paired electrical-fire choice.

C.text: Both foam and water can conduct electricity and expose the operator while equipment remains energised.

D.text: Carbon dioxide is suitable, but pairing it with water introduces an electrocution risk.

questions.prompt: What action should you take if you discover a fire?

options.A: Carry on working if it is safe to do so
options.B: Extinguish the fire without raising the alarm
options.C: Leave it because you will get the blame

questions.explanation: Raising the alarm will reduce the risk to others, particularly if the fire spreads.

A.text: Continuing work ignores an escalating emergency and prevents the site's fire procedure from starting.

B.text: Attempting extinction without warning people can delay evacuation and leave the worker trapped if the fire grows.

C.text: Fear of blame cannot justify leaving others unaware of a fire that may spread rapidly.

D.text: Raising the alarm will reduce the risk to others, particularly if the fire spreads.

questions.prompt: If there had been a small fire, who should you report it to?
questions.explanation: The supervisor should be aware, so that further preventative measures can be considered.

A.text: The main contractor may need notification through site arrangements, but the worker's immediate reporting line is the supervisor.

B.text: A resident engineer may have no responsibility for the worker or fire procedure and is not the normal first report.

C.text: The fire marshal manages evacuation duties; reporting through the supervisor ensures the incident is recorded and investigated.

D.text: The supervisor should be aware, so that further preventative measures can be considered.

questions.prompt: If you discover a fire at work, what should you do first:

options.A: Raise the alarm and warn fellow workers
options.B: Run around looking for an alarm to sound
options.D: Use a fire extinguisher to put it out

questions.explanation: Raising the alarm will reduce the risk to others, particularly if the fire spreads.

A.text: Raising the alarm will reduce the risk to others, particularly if the fire spreads.

B.text: Searching without immediately warning others delays evacuation; use the nearest recognised alarm method at once.

C.text: Emergency services should be called under the procedure, but people in immediate danger must first be alerted.

D.text: Trying to fight the fire before raising the alarm can trap the worker and leaves everyone else unaware.

questions.prompt: What is a fire assembly point?

options.A: A place where fire extinguishers are kept
options.B: A place where the fire brigade goes to
options.C: The place to go when the fire alarm sounds
options.D: The place where the fire alarm is

questions.explanation: The fire assembly point is the agreed safe place everyone goes to when the alarm sounds, so marshals can take a roll call and confirm no one is left inside the building.

A.text: Extinguisher points house equipment; they are not the safe location used to account for evacuated people.

B.text: Fire crews may establish their own rendezvous, but the workforce assembly point is for roll call after evacuation.

C.text: The fire assembly point is the agreed safe place everyone goes to when the alarm sounds, so marshals can take a roll call and confirm no one is left inside the building.

D.text: An alarm point initiates warning; it is not the place where occupants wait safely once warned.

questions.prompt: Where would you go in the event of a fire?

options.A: To the canteen for a cup of tea
options.C: To the fire to see what is going on

questions.explanation: On a fire you evacuate to the designated assembly point, where everyone can be accounted for. Returning to huts or the canteen, or approaching the fire, leaves you in danger and unaccounted for.

A.text: A canteen is not necessarily outside the danger area and prevents the fire roll call from accounting for you.

B.text: On a fire you evacuate to the designated assembly point, where everyone can be accounted for. Returning to huts or the canteen, or approaching the fire, leaves you in danger and unaccounted for.

C.text: Approaching the fire increases exposure to smoke, heat and structural danger and obstructs emergency responders.

D.text: A site hut is not a safe destination unless it is specifically designated as the assembly point.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you hear the fire alarm?

options.A: Evacuate the premises to a designated place of safety
options.B: Go towards the sound to find out what is going on
options.C: Ignore it because it might be someone playing around

questions.explanation: The alarm means leave at once by the nearest route to the designated place of safety. Investigating or ignoring it wastes vital escape time and puts your life at risk.

A.text: The alarm means leave at once by the nearest route to the designated place of safety. Investigating or ignoring it wastes vital escape time and puts your life at risk.

B.text: Moving toward the alarm can take the worker into smoke or fire and obstruct the response.

C.text: Every alarm must be treated as real until authorised otherwise; assuming a prank can be fatal.

D.text: Leaving for home bypasses the assembly-point roll call and may send the person through an unsafe route.

questions.prompt: An emergency route(s) must be provided on construction sites to ensure:

options.A: Safe passage to a secure place of safety
options.B: Safe passage to the ground from height
options.C: Safe passage to the open air
options.D: Safe passage to the rest area

questions.explanation: Emergency routes exist to get people away from danger to a defined place of safety, where they are secure and can be accounted for. Simply reaching open air or the ground is not enough if that spot is still within the hazard zone.

A.text: Emergency routes exist to get people away from danger to a defined place of safety, where they are secure and can be accounted for. Simply reaching open air or the ground is not enough if that spot is still within the hazard zone.

B.text: Reaching ground level addresses only escape from height and may still leave people inside the danger zone.

C.text: Open air is not automatically safe if it remains exposed to fire, smoke, collapse or another site emergency.

D.text: A rest area is provided for welfare, not necessarily as a protected destination during an emergency.

questions.prompt: The extended use of powered hand-held tools and equipment may lead to which medical condition?
questions.explanation: Hand-arm vibration can cause a range of conditions (including vibration white finger) collectively known as hand-arm vibration syndrome, as well as diseases such as carpal tunnel syndrome.

A.text: Asbestosis follows inhalation of asbestos fibres, not vibration transmitted from powered hand tools.

B.text: Dermatitis arises from skin irritants or allergens and is not the characteristic vascular and nerve effect of vibration.

C.text: Hand-arm vibration can cause a range of conditions (including vibration white finger) collectively known as hand-arm vibration syndrome, as well as diseases such as carpal tunnel syndrome.

D.text: Weil's disease is an infection associated with animal urine, wet ground and waterways, not tool vibration.

questions.prompt: What must your employer do if the daily personal noise exposure is at or exceeds 85 db(A)?

options.A: Issue hearing protection to those exposed and ensure that it is worn
options.B: Provide hearing protection to those employees who ask for it
options.C: Report it to the Health and Safety Executive
options.D: Tell employees to buy their own hearing protection

questions.explanation: This is an interim measure under the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 when the daily personal noise exposure is at or exceeds the upper exposure action value of 85 dB(A). Exposure should subsequently be reduced by implementing organizational or technical measures.

A.text: This is an interim measure under the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 when the daily personal noise exposure is at or exceeds the upper exposure action value of 85 dB(A). Exposure should subsequently be reduced by implementing organizational or technical measures.

B.text: Providing protection only on request applies at the lower action value; at 85 dB(A) its use must be ensured.

C.text: Crossing the upper action value requires exposure controls and hearing protection, not routine notification to HSE.

D.text: Required PPE must be supplied by the employer without charge; workers cannot be told to buy their own.

questions.prompt: What are the lower and upper action values with regard to daily personal noise exposure, as defined in the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005?
questions.explanation: Daily personal noise exposure is the average noise level experienced by an individual over an 8 hour period.

A.text: Seventy and eighty decibels understate both statutory exposure action values in the Noise Regulations.

B.text: The upper value is right, but the lower action value begins at 80 dB(A), not 75 dB(A).

C.text: Daily personal noise exposure is the average noise level experienced by an individual over an 8 hour period.

D.text: Eighty-five is the upper action value, not the lower one, and 90 dB(A) is not the current upper action value.

questions.prompt: At or above what level of daily personal noise exposure does an employer have to provide hearing protection if it is requested by an employee?
questions.explanation: This is one of the duties of employers under the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 when the lower exposure action value of 80 dB(A) is reached or exceeded.

A.text: This is one of the duties of employers under the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 when the lower exposure action value of 80 dB(A) is reached or exceeded.

B.text: At 85 dB(A) the employer must ensure hearing protection is used; provision on request starts at the lower value.

C.text: Ninety decibels is above both action values and is not the threshold at which requested protection first becomes available.

D.text: Ninety-five decibels is an extremely high exposure and delaying protection until then would ignore both action values.

questions.prompt: The effects of damage to your hearing by long-term exposure to high noise levels:

options.B: Can be corrected by an operation
options.C: Can be reversed to near normal, with time
options.D: Will be reduced when you change jobs

questions.explanation: Loud noise destroys the tiny hair cells in the inner ear, and these do not regrow. Once that damage happens it is permanent, which is why hearing protection and reducing exposure matter so much.

A.text: Loud noise destroys the tiny hair cells in the inner ear, and these do not regrow. Once that damage happens it is permanent, which is why hearing protection and reducing exposure matter so much.

B.text: Noise-damaged inner-ear hair cells are not restored by a routine operation.

C.text: Temporary threshold shift can recover, but established long-term noise-induced hearing loss does not return to normal.

D.text: Changing jobs can stop further exposure but cannot reverse damage that has already occurred.

questions.prompt: Hearing protection should be worn:
questions.explanation: Employees must wear hearing protectors when exposed at or above the upper exposure action values and within hearing protection zones.

A.text: Universal wear can overprotect workers and interfere with communication where the noise assessment does not require it.

B.text: Employees must wear hearing protectors when exposed at or above the upper exposure action values and within hearing protection zones.

C.text: Hazardous noise occurs outdoors as well as indoors, so building enclosure is not the deciding factor.

D.text: Factories, workshops and many other workplaces also designate hearing-protection zones; the rule is not site-specific.

questions.prompt: Wearing suitable hearing protection:

options.A: Brings noise down to an acceptable level

questions.explanation: Hearing protection still allows some noise to reach the ear, but, if it has been correctly chosen, will reduce noise levels to an acceptable level.

A.text: Hearing protection still allows some noise to reach the ear, but, if it has been correctly chosen, will reduce noise levels to an acceptable level.

B.text: Hearing protection prevents further exposure; it cannot repair sensory cells already damaged by noise.

C.text: Suitable protectors attenuate noise rather than eliminating all sound, allowing essential warnings to remain audible.

D.text: Conversation reduction may occur, but selection is based on hazardous noise exposure rather than social distraction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is one of the recommended means of protecting your hearing?
questions.explanation: The others are not considered to be suitable types of hearing protection.

A.text: Loose cotton wool has no tested attenuation, fit or repeatable seal and is not certified hearing PPE.

B.text: The others are not considered to be suitable types of hearing protection.

C.text: Rolled tissue provides unpredictable, inadequate attenuation and can lodge in the ear canal.

D.text: Cloth pads do not seal the ear or provide a rated reduction across hazardous frequencies.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would not reduce the risks from hand-arm vibration when using a hammer-action tool?

options.A: Making sure one person does all the work with the tool
options.B: Selecting the lowest vibration tool that is suitable and which can do the work efficiently
options.C: Wearing gloves to keep the hands warm
options.D: Working as a team to share the work out

questions.explanation: Where tools require constant or frequent use, rotas will avoid individuals having long exposure to vibration. The use of low-vibration tools and keeping the hands warm in cold conditions will also reduce the risks.

A.text: Where tools require constant or frequent use, rotas will avoid individuals having long exposure to vibration. The use of low-vibration tools and keeping the hands warm in cold conditions will also reduce the risks.

B.text: A lower-vibration efficient tool reduces the vibration magnitude and often the trigger time for the task.

C.text: Warm gloves do not absorb significant vibration, but keeping hands warm can reduce painful vascular symptoms.

D.text: Sharing planned exposure reduces each person's trigger time when other controls cannot eliminate the work.

questions.prompt: Which of the following animals can carry Weil's disease?
questions.explanation: Weil's disease is a serious and sometimes fatal infection that can be transmitted to humans by contact with infected rats. Another form of Leptospirosis infection can be transmitted from cattle to humans.

A.text: Pigs can carry other zoonoses, but rats and their urine are the classic construction-site source of Weil's disease.

B.text: Weil's disease is a serious and sometimes fatal infection that can be transmitted to humans by contact with infected rats. Another form of Leptospirosis infection can be transmitted from cattle to humans.

C.text: Sheep are associated with different occupational infections; they are not the expected reservoir in this question.

D.text: Snake exposure is unrelated to leptospiral infection from urine-contaminated water or wet ground.

questions.prompt: You are most likely to catch Weil's disease (Leptospirosis) if you:

options.D: Work near wet ground, waterways or sewers

questions.explanation: Anyone who is exposed to rat urine is at risk, particularly sewer workers and farmers. Those in contact with canal or river water are also at risk.

A.text: A maintained wholesome standpipe is not the typical rat-urine exposure route described for leptospirosis.

B.text: Installing domestic sanitary fittings does not inherently expose a worker to infected water or rat urine.

C.text: Air-conditioning work is associated with other biological risks, not the usual wet-ground source of Weil's disease.

D.text: Anyone who is exposed to rat urine is at risk, particularly sewer workers and farmers. Those in contact with canal or river water are also at risk.

questions.prompt: What should you do if the toilets on your site are continually dirty?

options.A: Ask in a nearby cafe or pub if you can use their toilets
options.B: Find some cleaning materials and clean it up yourself
options.C: Ignore the problem - its normal on a construction site
options.D: Make sure you tell someone who can sort it out

questions.explanation: How often welfare facilities on site require cleaning will depend on the number of people on site and how quickly they get dirty. The person in control of the site should make sure someone is responsible for keeping the facilities clean and tidy.

A.text: Using a nearby business shifts the welfare burden elsewhere and does not correct the employer-provided facilities.

B.text: Workers should leave sanitation and hazardous cleaning to the arranged service rather than silently taking it on themselves.

C.text: Persistent dirt is not normal or acceptable; it can spread illness and shows that welfare maintenance is failing.

D.text: How often welfare facilities on site require cleaning will depend on the number of people on site and how quickly they get dirty. The person in control of the site should make sure someone is responsible for keeping the facilities clean and tidy.

questions.prompt: Excessive sunlight on bare skin can cause which serious health problem?
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet rays in sunlight can cause sunburn and premature ageing of the skin. The most serious effect, however, is an increased chance of developing skin cancer.

A.text: Acne is not the principal serious disease linked to cumulative ultraviolet exposure from working in strong sunlight.

B.text: Some exposures cause dermatitis, but ultraviolet radiation's major long-term danger is malignant skin change.

C.text: Rickets is associated with vitamin D deficiency, not excessive ultraviolet exposure to bare skin.

D.text: Ultraviolet rays in sunlight can cause sunburn and premature ageing of the skin. The most serious effect, however, is an increased chance of developing skin cancer.

questions.prompt: Exposure to asbestos fibres may cause which one of the following?
questions.explanation: Breathing in asbestos fibres can also lead to a number of other diseases, including lung cancer and mesothelioma

A.text: Breathing in asbestos fibres can also lead to a number of other diseases, including lung cancer and mesothelioma

B.text: Asthma can have many workplace causes, but it is not the characteristic fibrotic lung disease caused by asbestos fibres.

C.text: Dermatitis is an inflammatory skin condition; inhaled asbestos primarily causes serious diseases of the lungs and pleura.

D.text: Glandular fever is a viral infection and has no causal link to breathing asbestos fibres.

questions.prompt: Asbestos is suspected in the workplace, during renovation do you:
questions.explanation: Competent advice must be sought, to prevent exposure to the worker or others, either at the time, or subsequently.

A.text: Ignoring suspected asbestos can release fibres during further disturbance and expose everyone in the work area.

B.text: Painting does not identify the material or make unplanned drilling, cutting or removal safe.

C.text: Removal is licensed or specially controlled work in many circumstances and must not start on suspicion alone.

D.text: Competent advice must be sought, to prevent exposure to the worker or others, either at the time, or subsequently.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about asbestos is TRUE?

options.A: All forms of asbestos can cause fatal diseases.
options.B: Asbestos is not really a hazard to health
options.C: Only brown and blue asbestos are a hazard to health
options.D: White asbestos is safe to use

questions.explanation: All forms of asbestos can cause fatal diseases. is correct because asbestos exposure can cause fatal disease and must be controlled by trained, authorised people. You should avoid disturbing suspect material and follow the site procedure immediately.

A.text: All forms of asbestos can cause fatal diseases. is correct because asbestos exposure can cause fatal disease and must be controlled by trained, authorised people. You should avoid disturbing suspect material and follow the site procedure immediately.

B.text: Asbestos exposure can cause mesothelioma, lung cancer and asbestosis years later, even when no immediate symptom occurs.

C.text: White asbestos can also cause fatal disease; fibre colour does not make chrysotile exposure safe.

D.text: No asbestos type is safe to disturb or use without the applicable controls, including white chrysotile.

questions.prompt: While working you discover material you think could be asbestos. What should you do?

options.A: Clear any dust and fragments, put them in a bin then carry on working
options.B: Dampen the material to prevent further dust being created, then carry on working
options.D: Stop working immediately and report your suspicions to your supervisor

questions.explanation: It is essential to stop work if asbestos is found or suspected, and await competent advice on what to do next.

A.text: Sweeping and binning fragments can release fibres and creates unlicensed, uncontained asbestos waste.

B.text: Damping alone does not identify the material or authorise continued disturbance under an assessed method.

C.text: A nurse may later advise on exposure, but the work area first needs to be stopped and controlled through supervision.

D.text: It is essential to stop work if asbestos is found or suspected, and await competent advice on what to do next.

questions.prompt: Can you tell by the smell of a product whether it is likely to cause harm?

options.B: Only if you have been trained

questions.explanation: Smell is no guide to safety. Many harmful substances are odourless, while others numb your sense of smell or seem pleasant. You must rely on the safety data sheet and labelling, never your nose, to judge whether something is dangerous.

A.text: Smell is no guide to safety. Many harmful substances are odourless, while others numb your sense of smell or seem pleasant. You must rely on the safety data sheet and labelling, never your nose, to judge whether something is dangerous.

B.text: Training helps interpret labels and controls, but it cannot make odour a reliable detector of toxicity.

C.text: Enclosure may concentrate vapour, yet harmful products can be odourless or detectable only after unsafe exposure.

D.text: Pleasant, weak or absent smell does not indicate low toxicity, and olfactory fatigue can remove warning.

questions.prompt: How would you recognise a hazardous substance?

options.A: By the hazard pictograms and other warning information on its label and safety data sheet
options.C: It will be in a suitable container
options.D: The colour of the label on the container

questions.explanation: Hazardous chemicals are identified from their classified label information, including pictograms, signal words and hazard statements, supported by the safety data sheet. Smell, container appearance or label colour alone is not a reliable test.

A.text: Hazardous chemicals are identified from their classified label information, including pictograms, signal words and hazard statements, supported by the safety data sheet. Smell, container appearance or label colour alone is not a reliable test.

B.text: Odour is subjective, may be absent and can occur only above a harmful exposure concentration.

C.text: Safe packaging does not mean the contents are harmless; hazardous substances should also be stored in suitable containers.

D.text: Label background colour is not the classification system; pictograms, signal words and hazard statements carry the warning.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does NOT cause skin problems?
questions.explanation: Asbestos is correct because asbestos exposure can cause fatal disease and must be controlled by trained, authorised people. You should avoid disturbing suspect material and follow the site procedure immediately.

A.text: Asbestos is correct because asbestos exposure can cause fatal disease and must be controlled by trained, authorised people. You should avoid disturbing suspect material and follow the site procedure immediately.

B.text: Bitumen and its solvents can irritate skin and cause dermatitis, especially with repeated hot-material contact.

C.text: Epoxy resins are potent skin sensitisers and can produce persistent allergic contact dermatitis.

D.text: Solvents remove natural skin oils and can cause irritation, dryness and occupational dermatitis.

questions.prompt: When an assessment of hazardous substances has been carried out under the COSHH Regulations, the risks and control measures should be explained to:

options.D: the person in charge of the stores

questions.explanation: All those working with the hazardous substances in question need to know about any risks.

A.text: People who never use or encounter the substance do not need task-specific detail; information must reach everyone who may actually be exposed.

B.text: Accounts staff deal with purchasing and payment, not the exposure controls needed at the point of use.

C.text: All those working with the hazardous substances in question need to know about any risks.

D.text: The storekeeper needs safe-storage information, but that alone leaves the operatives handling the substance uninformed.

questions.prompt: If your hands are very dirty, what should you use to get them clean?
questions.explanation: Soap and water cleans skin without harming it. Solvents like paraffin, thinners and white spirit strip the skin's natural oils, can be absorbed into the body, and cause dermatitis, so they must never be used to wash hands.

A.text: Paraffin dissolves the skin's protective oils and can cause irritation or dermatitis, so it is not a hand cleaner.

B.text: Soap and water cleans skin without harming it. Solvents like paraffin, thinners and white spirit strip the skin's natural oils, can be absorbed into the body, and cause dermatitis, so they must never be used to wash hands.

C.text: Paint thinner is a solvent that can damage skin and allow harmful chemicals to be absorbed.

D.text: White spirit strips natural oils from the skin; contamination should be removed with suitable soap and water instead.

questions.prompt: The presence of rats on site creates a risk of catching Weil's disease. What is the EASIEST PRACTICAL MEASURE that you can take to discourage the presence of rats?

options.A: Avoid leaving scraps of food lying about
options.B: Bring a large cat on site
options.C: Contact the local Environmental Health Officer

questions.explanation: The easiest solution is to avoid leaving food around, since this is what attracts vermin.

A.text: The easiest solution is to avoid leaving food around, since this is what attracts vermin.

B.text: An uncontrolled animal creates new welfare and site-safety problems and is not a reliable pest-control measure.

C.text: Environmental health can advise on an infestation, but removing exposed food is the immediate practical prevention step available to each worker.

D.text: Poison and traps require competent pest control and safe placement; casually laying bait can harm people and other animals.

questions.prompt: Why is personal hygiene so important?

options.A: Because the COSHH regulations require it

B.text: Installing domestic sanitary fittings does not inherently expose a worker to infected water or rat urine.

C.text: Air-conditioning work is associated with other biological risks, not the usual wet-ground source of Weil's disease.

D.text: Anyone who is exposed to rat urine is at risk, particularly sewer workers and farmers. Those in contact with canal or river water are also at risk.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about asbestos is TRUE?

options.A: All forms of asbestos can cause fatal diseases.
options.B: Asbestos is not really a hazard to health
options.C: Only brown and blue asbestos are a hazard to health
options.D: White asbestos is safe to use

questions.explanation: All types of asbestos, including white chrysotile as well as brown and blue, release fibres that can cause fatal diseases such as mesothelioma and asbestosis. There is no safe variety, which is why every form must be treated as a serious health hazard.

A.text: All types of asbestos, including white chrysotile as well as brown and blue, release fibres that can cause fatal diseases such as mesothelioma and asbestosis. There is no safe variety, which is why every form must be treated as a serious health hazard.

B.text: Asbestos exposure can cause mesothelioma, lung cancer and asbestosis years later, even when no immediate symptom occurs.

C.text: White asbestos can also cause fatal disease; fibre colour does not make chrysotile exposure safe.

D.text: No asbestos type is safe to disturb or use without the applicable controls, including white chrysotile.

questions.prompt: The presence of rats on site creates a risk of catching Weil's disease. What is the EASIEST PRACTICAL MEASURE that you can take to discourage the presence of rats?

options.A: Avoid leaving scraps of food lying about
options.B: Bring a large cat on site
options.C: Contact the local Environmental Health Officer

questions.explanation: The easiest solution is to avoid leaving food around, since this is what attracts vermin.

A.text: The easiest solution is to avoid leaving food around, since this is what attracts vermin.

B.text: An uncontrolled animal creates new welfare and site-safety problems and is not a reliable pest-control measure.

C.text: Environmental health can advise on an infestation, but removing exposed food is the immediate practical prevention step available to each worker.

D.text: Poison and traps require competent pest control and safe placement; casually laying bait can harm people and other animals.

questions.prompt: If it is necessary for an employee to use personal protective equipment, who has a duty to provide it?
questions.explanation: This is a requirement of the PPE at Work Regulations 1992 (Regulation 4).

A.text: A worker must use and care for PPE, but the legal duty to select and supply it rests with the employer.

B.text: This is a requirement of the PPE at Work Regulations 1992 (Regulation 4).

C.text: A principal contractor coordinates site-wide arrangements, but each employer remains responsible for PPE needed by its own workers.

D.text: A trade union may represent workers and raise concerns, but it does not purchase statutory PPE on the employer's behalf.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following should you do if your personal protective equipment (PPE) is damaged?

options.C: Reduce the amount of time you use it
options.D: Report to your Supervisor without delay

questions.explanation: Employees are required to report any defective PPE to their employer (PPE at Work Regulations 1992, Regulation 7)

A.text: Continuing with damaged PPE leaves the identified hazard uncontrolled exactly when protection may be needed.

B.text: Waiting for a convenient replacement exposes the worker in the meantime; use should stop and the defect be reported.

C.text: Shorter exposure does not restore the equipment's protection or make an unknown failure mode predictable.

D.text: Employees are required to report any defective PPE to their employer (PPE at Work Regulations 1992, Regulation 7)

questions.prompt: When MUST an employer provide their employees with personal protective equipment (PPE)?

options.B: If the client or main contractor specifies it in the contract
options.D: When they may be exposed to a risk to their health & safety which cannot be controlled another way

questions.explanation: PPE sits at the bottom of the hierarchy of control, so an employer must supply it whenever a risk to health and safety cannot be adequately eliminated or controlled by other means. It is provided to address residual risk, not on a fixed schedule or because a contract demands it.

A.text: PPE provision responds to the present residual risk, not a five-year replacement timetable.

B.text: A contract may add site rules, but the employer's statutory duty exists even when the client says nothing about PPE.

C.text: Inspection and replacement intervals depend on the equipment and condition; twice-yearly issue is not the legal trigger.

D.text: PPE sits at the bottom of the hierarchy of control, so an employer must supply it whenever a risk to health and safety cannot be adequately eliminated or controlled by other means. It is provided to address residual risk, not on a fixed schedule or because a contract demands it.

questions.prompt: You have witnessed a serious accident on your site and are interviewed by an HSE inspector. Should you:

options.A: Ask your supervisor what you should say to the inspector
options.B: Co-operate fully with the inspector and tell him exactly what you saw
options.D: Tell the inspector what your mates say you should tell him

questions.explanation: This is good practice, but it can also be an offence to withhold important information from an inspector.

A.text: A witness should give an independent factual account; rehearsing it with a supervisor risks distorting evidence.

B.text: This is good practice, but it can also be an offence to withhold important information from an inspector.

C.text: Withholding relevant facts obstructs the investigation and may itself amount to an offence.

D.text: Second-hand suggestions are not evidence; the inspector needs what the witness personally saw and heard.

questions.prompt: A workmate tells you that he witnessed an accident the previous day and the victim was taken to hospital. He asks you for advice on what he should do. Do you tell him to:

options.A: Say nothing to anyone in case he gets someone in trouble
options.B: Speak to the site nurse about what he saw
options.C: Telephone the hospital to find out how the injured person is
options.D: Tell his supervisor that he saw what happened

questions.explanation: If the supervisor is aware of an accident he can take steps to prevent a recurrence. The employer also has legal duties to report certain incidents to the enforcing authority.

A.text: Silence protects neither the injured person nor co-workers and can allow the same uncontrolled hazard to injure someone else.

B.text: A nurse deals with treatment; the supervisor needs the witness account so the workplace event can be investigated.

C.text: Checking the casualty's condition does not report the evidence or help the employer control the cause.

D.text: If the supervisor is aware of an accident he can take steps to prevent a recurrence. The employer also has legal duties to report certain incidents to the enforcing authority.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct way to lift a load?

options.A: Keep feet apart and bend back
options.B: Keep feet together and bend back
options.C: Squat near load, bend back and use leg muscles
options.D: Adopt a stable stance, get a secure hold, keep the load close and use slight bending of the back, hips and knees without twisting or further back flexion

questions.explanation: HSE advises a stable foot position, a secure hold, keeping the load close and slight bending of the back, hips and knees. A full deep squat or a deliberately bent back is not the universal correct technique, and handling technique does not replace risk reduction or lifting aids.

A.text: Bending mainly through the back while holding a load away from the body increases spinal leverage and instability.

B.text: Feet together provide a narrow, unstable base, and deliberate back bending increases strain.

C.text: A deep squat with a bent back is not a universal safe method and may create high knee and back loads.

D.text: HSE advises a stable foot position, a secure hold, keeping the load close and slight bending of the back, hips and knees. A full deep squat or a deliberately bent back is not the universal correct technique, and handling technique does not replace risk reduction or lifting aids.

questions.prompt: What immediate action should you take if you suffer an injury through carrying a load?

options.A: Advise your doctor of your injury
options.B: Carry on working as best you can

questions.explanation: All injuries must be recorded in the Company accident book (BI 510).

A.text: Medical advice may be needed, but the workplace must first know about the injury so help, recording and controls can be arranged.

B.text: Continuing can worsen a strain and prevents assessment of the handling task that caused it.

C.text: All injuries must be recorded in the Company accident book (BI 510).

D.text: A companion cannot authorise treatment or change the system of work; the supervisor or employer needs the report.

questions.prompt: Where a load has to be lifted manually, what is the employer required to do by law?

options.A: Assess the risk of the task
options.B: Assess the time the job will take
options.C: Calculate the cost of the exercise
options.D: Determine the number of people required

questions.explanation: This is a specific requirement of the Manual Handling Operations regulations 1992.

A.text: This is a specific requirement of the Manual Handling Operations regulations 1992.

B.text: Duration can affect exposure but does not replace the required assessment of likelihood and severity of injury.

C.text: Cost planning says nothing about posture, load stability, route or worker capability.

D.text: Team size is one possible control to consider after assessment, not the legal assessment itself.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would NOT make a load easier to handle manually

options.B: Providing suitable handles or hand grips
options.D: Securing the load so that it does not shift unexpectedly

questions.explanation: Manual handling risk is reduced by making a load lighter, easier to grip and stable so it cannot shift unexpectedly. Painting it a bright colour changes none of these physical characteristics, so it does nothing to make the load easier or safer to lift and carry.

A.text: Manual handling risk is reduced by making a load lighter, easier to grip and stable so it cannot shift unexpectedly. Painting it a bright colour changes none of these physical characteristics, so it does nothing to make the load easier or safer to lift and carry.

B.text: Purpose-designed grips improve control and reduce the force needed to prevent the load slipping.

C.text: Reducing weight directly lowers the muscular force and spinal loading involved in handling.

D.text: Restraint prevents an internal or loose load shifting suddenly and pulling the handler off balance.

questions.prompt: How can you help to prevent accidents?

options.B: Know how to get help quickly
options.C: Know where the first-aid kit is kept

questions.explanation: Action to improve safety can only be taken if the risk is known about. Employees have a duty of care to other employees.

A.text: Suppressing incident reports hides patterns and prevents management from removing the cause.

B.text: Knowing how to summon help limits harm after an event but does not remove the unsafe condition that causes it.

C.text: First-aid readiness improves response after injury; prevention requires hazards to be reported and controlled beforehand.

D.text: Action to improve safety can only be taken if the risk is known about. Employees have a duty of care to other employees.

questions.prompt: Which is the part of your body MOST LIKELY to be injured during a manual handling activity which involves moving a heavy load?
questions.explanation: Lifting and moving heavy loads places the greatest strain on the lower back, where poor posture and twisting can damage the spine and supporting muscles. This makes back injury the most common manual handling injury, which good lifting technique is designed to prevent.

A.text: Lifting and moving heavy loads places the greatest strain on the lower back, where poor posture and twisting can damage the spine and supporting muscles. This makes back injury the most common manual handling injury, which good lifting technique is designed to prevent.

B.text: Chest injury is possible in a crush event, but ordinary heavy handling most commonly overloads the back and supporting tissues.

C.text: Forearms can fatigue while gripping, yet the spine usually bears the greater injury risk from load leverage and twisting.

D.text: Knees can be stressed by poor posture, but back injury is the most common concern across heavy manual-handling tasks.

questions.prompt: For relevant Health and Safety at Work etc. Act offences tried on indictment, which listed maximum penalties can a Crown Court impose on an individual?

options.B: An unlimited fine and up to two years' imprisonment
options.D: An unlimited fine and six months' imprisonment

questions.explanation: For relevant offences tried on indictment, the available maximum is an unlimited fine and, for an individual, imprisonment up to two years, or both. The original term 'Higher Court' was imprecise and not every offence or defendant attracts identical sentencing powers.

A.text: A £1,000 cap and six-month term understate the current Crown Court maxima for the relevant offences.

B.text: For relevant offences tried on indictment, the available maximum is an unlimited fine and, for an individual, imprisonment up to two years, or both. The original term 'Higher Court' was imprecise and not every offence or defendant attracts identical sentencing powers.

C.text: The fine is not capped at £20,000 when tried on indictment, even though two years may be the custodial maximum.

D.text: The fine can be unlimited, but the listed six-month custody term is below the relevant two-year maximum.

questions.prompt: A Health and Safety Executive Inspector can?

options.A: Only visit if accompanied by the principal contractor
options.B: Only visit if they have made an appointment
options.C: Only visit to interview the site manager
options.D: Enter premises at any reasonable time, or at any time when the inspector believes a dangerous situation exists

questions.explanation: HSWA section 20 empowers an appointed inspector to enter at any reasonable time, and at any time where the inspector has reasonable cause to believe a dangerous situation exists. 'Visit at any time' without that qualification overstated the ordinary power.

A.text: The inspector's statutory entry power does not depend on the principal contractor accompanying the visit.

B.text: Requiring an appointment would allow dangerous conditions to be hidden and is not a condition in section 20.

C.text: Inspectors may examine premises, evidence, articles and people; their power is not limited to one manager interview.

D.text: HSWA section 20 empowers an appointed inspector to enter at any reasonable time, and at any time where the inspector has reasonable cause to believe a dangerous situation exists. 'Visit at any time' without that qualification overstated the ordinary power.

questions.prompt: Employers are required to provide information to their employees on their health and safety rights and responsibilities and how to get advice by:

options.A: Displaying a poster or giving them leaflets approved by the HSE
options.C: Making them read the company health and safety policy
options.D: Telling them verbally when they start work for them

questions.explanation: This is a requirement of the Health and Safety Information for Employees Regulations (as amended).

A.text: This is a requirement of the Health and Safety Information for Employees Regulations (as amended).

B.text: An ordinary email is not one of the prescribed methods unless it supplies the approved leaflet itself in an acceptable way.

C.text: The company policy explains local arrangements but does not replace the official law poster or approved employee leaflet.

D.text: A verbal induction can add site detail, but it does not satisfy the separate duty to provide the approved rights information.

questions.prompt: The Health and Safety Executive is:

options.A: Part of the National Health Service
options.C: The jury in health and safety court cases
options.D: The regulatory body for the promotion of health and safety at work

questions.explanation: The Health and Safety Executive is part of the Department for Work and Pensions.

A.text: The NHS provides healthcare, whereas HSE regulates work-related health and safety risks.

B.text: Police investigate criminal matters but are not the specialist workplace health and safety regulator.

C.text: A jury decides facts in a particular court case; HSE investigates and enforces across workplaces before any trial.

D.text: The Health and Safety Executive is part of the Department for Work and Pensions.

questions.prompt: Intumescent materials used to provide fire-stopping are designed to:
questions.explanation: A limited number of fire-resistant materials may be used to provide fire-stopping. These include intumescent products, which are designed to expand and provide fire-stopping when subjected to heat. Examples include intumescent 'pillows' (used to provide internal sealing of trunking) and intumescent mastic.

A.text: A limited number of fire-resistant materials may be used to provide fire-stopping. These include intumescent products, which are designed to expand and provide fire-stopping when subjected to heat. Examples include intumescent 'pillows' (used to provide internal sealing of trunking) and intumescent mastic.

B.text: Intumescent compounds react to elevated temperature, not merely to the presence of smoke particles.

C.text: Blocking sound is an acoustic treatment and does not describe the heat-driven action of an intumescent product.

D.text: Shrinking would enlarge the penetration during a fire; intumescent material must swell to close the opening.

questions.prompt: When storing liquids (such as oils, fuels or chemicals) on-site, what must you do?

options.B: Store them in suitable closed and labelled containers, securely and away from traffic, with containment such as a bund or drip tray where leakage could pollute
options.C: Keep the tops off, to prevent pressure from building up
options.D: Use a transparent container so you can check how much liquid is in it

questions.explanation: Site liquids must be stored in suitable compatible containers, identified and secured against damage or unauthorised access. Where a leak could pollute land or drains, appropriate secondary containment is also needed; simply putting a container out of traffic is not enough.

A.text: The nearest container may be incompatible, unlabelled or damaged and cannot be chosen merely for convenience.

B.text: Site liquids must be stored in suitable compatible containers, identified and secured against damage or unauthorised access. Where a leak could pollute land or drains, appropriate secondary containment is also needed; simply putting a container out of traffic is not enough.

C.text: Open containers allow vapour, rain ingress and spills and are not a safe means of relieving pressure.

D.text: Transparency does not establish compatibility, labelling, security or secondary containment for a hazardous liquid.

questions.prompt: Other site workers are complaining that you are generating too much dust. What should you do?

options.A: Ignore them - it's none of their business
options.B: Issue the other site workers with dust masks
options.C: Stop work and inform your supervisor
options.D: Tell them you have nearly finished

questions.explanation: Excessive dust may be a health hazard to you and those around you, but even if it is not a health hazard, excessive dust can be a 'statutory nuisance (under the Environmental Protection Act). Even when it is not a statutory nuisance, it can lead to complaints from neighbours and possible damage to neighbouring property.

A.text: Dust affects other workers and can escape the site, so their exposure is directly part of the duty holder's concern.

B.text: Issuing masks to everyone relies on PPE and does not control dust at source or address environmental nuisance.

C.text: Excessive dust may be a health hazard to you and those around you, but even if it is not a health hazard, excessive dust can be a 'statutory nuisance (under the Environmental Protection Act). Even when it is not a statutory nuisance, it can lead to complaints from neighbours and possible damage to neighbouring property.

D.text: A short remaining duration can still create a harmful peak exposure and is no reason to continue uncontrolled work.

questions.prompt: The Electricity at Work Regulations require that:

options.A: A training course is necessary before anyone can work with electricity
options.B: Anyone supervised can work with electricity
options.C: Only electricians can work with electricity
options.D: People must have adequate knowledge or experience, or be under an appropriate degree of supervision, to prevent danger and injury

questions.explanation: Regulation 16 permits work where technical knowledge or experience is necessary only when the person has that competence or is under an appropriate degree of supervision. It does not require every worker to already possess the same unsupervised competence.

A.text: A course may contribute to competence, but the Regulation focuses on effective knowledge, experience or supervision.

B.text: Supervision must be appropriate to prevent danger; the mere presence of any supervisor is not enough.

C.text: Job title is not the legal test, and non-electricians may do limited work when competence or supervision is adequate.

D.text: Regulation 16 permits work where technical knowledge or experience is necessary only when the person has that competence or is under an appropriate degree of supervision. It does not require every worker to already possess the same unsupervised competence.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a suitable means of isolating a circuit?

options.A: Fitting a padlocked circuit breaker lockout
options.C: Removing a fuse and securing the distribution board against access
options.D: Putting insulating tape over the circuit breaker instead of applying a secure lock-off device

questions.explanation: Tape does not secure an isolating device against inadvertent or unauthorised operation. HSE construction guidance explicitly contrasts tape over a circuit-breaker with a proper lock-off device, personal lock and safety notice.

A.text: A purpose-made circuit-breaker lockout and padlock secure the device against inadvertent operation.

B.text: Padlocking a suitable isolating switch provides the positive security that a safe isolation needs.

C.text: Removing the fuse and securing access can disconnect the circuit and prevent unauthorised replacement under the procedure.

D.text: Tape does not secure an isolating device against inadvertent or unauthorised operation. HSE construction guidance explicitly contrasts tape over a circuit-breaker with a proper lock-off device, personal lock and safety notice.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is classed as hazardous/special waste?
questions.explanation: Hazardous wastes (special wastes in Scotland) are specified in waste legislation. Fluorescent tubes are included because of their mercury content.

A.text: Empty cement bags are normally a non-hazardous construction waste stream when uncontaminated and correctly segregated.

B.text: Hazardous wastes (special wastes in Scotland) are specified in waste legislation. Fluorescent tubes are included because of their mercury content.

C.text: Non-asbestos insulation is not automatically hazardous, although dust and product-specific controls may still be needed.

D.text: Clean polythene and shrink wrap are generally segregated for recycling rather than treated as hazardous waste.

questions.prompt: Where there is no local means of isolation for equipment or circuits to be worked on, which of the following is the preferred method of isolation?

options.A: Disconnecting the individual circuit from the DB
options.B: Isolation of the individual circuit breaker or fuse
options.C: Isolation of the main switch or DB switch- disconnector
options.D: Pulling out the distributor's cut-out fuse

questions.explanation: Where no local isolator exists, isolating at the main switch or distribution board switch-disconnector provides a single, secure point that can be locked off under your control. This breaks the supply to everything downstream safely without disturbing the supplier's cut-out, which must never be tampered with.

A.text: Disconnecting conductors at the board is more intrusive and unnecessary where the board's main isolator can secure all supplies.

B.text: The premise states there is no local circuit isolation, so relying on an individual breaker or fuse does not solve it.

C.text: Where no local isolator exists, isolating at the main switch or distribution board switch-disconnector provides a single, secure point that can be locked off under your control. This breaks the supply to everything downstream safely without disturbing the supplier's cut-out, which must never be tampered with.

D.text: The distributor's sealed cut-out is not for ordinary contractors to remove and may expose dangerous live parts.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true with regard to the dangers of electricity?

options.A: Electricity is dangerous at any time because you cannot tell by looking at a cable whether or not it is live
options.B: Electricity is only dangerous if you are not wearing wellington boots
options.C: Electricity is only dangerous in wet weather
options.D: Electricity is perfectly safe so long as you wear cotton gloves

questions.explanation: The features which make electricity so dangerous are that you cannot see, hear or smell it. It can give you a very unpleasant surprise. Always assume that cables are live.

A.text: The features which make electricity so dangerous are that you cannot see, hear or smell it. It can give you a very unpleasant surprise. Always assume that cables are live.

B.text: Wellington boots are not a universal electrical safeguard and may be wet, damaged or unsuitable for the voltage.

C.text: Dry weather does not prove a conductor dead or remove the possibility of a fatal current path.

D.text: Cotton gloves have no electrical insulating rating and do not make contact with energised parts safe.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would you use to replace the fuse in a plug if fuses were NOT available?
questions.explanation: A fuse is often the main safety device in an electrical circuit. A blown fuse must only be replaced by a fuse of the correct type and rating.

A.text: A wire link has unknown current characteristics and can allow the flex or appliance to overheat and catch fire.

B.text: A nail will not melt safely under fault current and can leave the plug and cable without overcurrent protection.

C.text: Silver paper can bridge the fuse clips indefinitely, creating overheating and shock risk instead of controlled disconnection.

D.text: A fuse is often the main safety device in an electrical circuit. A blown fuse must only be replaced by a fuse of the correct type and rating.

questions.prompt: The lowest level of electrical current which can harm the human body is normally measured in:
questions.explanation: Research has shown that a person is in serious danger of a fatal electric shock at, or above, approximately 30 milliamps.

A.text: Whole amperes are far above the range where shock can already disrupt breathing or heart rhythm.

B.text: Kiloamperes describe fault-current magnitudes, not the small body current capable of causing physiological injury.

C.text: Microamperes are one-thousandth of a milliampere and are generally below the ordinary harmful-shock thresholds discussed.

D.text: Research has shown that a person is in serious danger of a fatal electric shock at, or above, approximately 30 milliamps.

questions.prompt: To determine the safety of the atmosphere in an excavation, which of the following is essential

options.B: Only entering for a short period to enable a quick escape

questions.explanation: Use a suitable detector. Many dangerous gases have no smell, and cannot be seen. Workers can be overcome in seconds in dangerous atmospheres.

A.text: Toxic gases and oxygen deficiency are often invisible, so visual inspection cannot establish atmospheric safety.

B.text: A dangerous atmosphere can overcome a worker before a quick escape is possible, even during a short entry.

C.text: Smell is unreliable and the attempt exposes the worker; some lethal gases have no detectable odour.

D.text: Use a suitable detector. Many dangerous gases have no smell, and cannot be seen. Workers can be overcome in seconds in dangerous atmospheres.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of using a 'permit to work' system?

options.A: To enable tools and equipment to be properly checked before the commencement of work
options.B: To ensure that the client will pay for the work
options.C: To ensure the job is carried out by the quickest method
options.D: To help ensure a safe system of work

questions.explanation: A permit to work is a written system used to control certain types of hazardous work. They allow work to start only when site procedures have been clarified.

A.text: Tool checks may be included, but a permit principally coordinates hazards, isolations, boundaries and authorisation for the work.

B.text: Payment belongs to the contract and is unrelated to the permit's control of hazardous work.

C.text: Speed is not the permit's objective and can conflict with the deliberate checks required for safe execution.

D.text: A permit to work is a written system used to control certain types of hazardous work. They allow work to start only when site procedures have been clarified.

questions.prompt: A Cable Avoidance Tool (C.A.T.) and a 'Genny' (generator) can be used successfully to locate underground cables by whom:
questions.explanation: Equipment used to locate buried services must only be used by people who have been trained to use it.

A.text: Equipment used to locate buried services must only be used by people who have been trained to use it.

B.text: Employment by an electricity company does not prove training on the particular locator or site conditions.

C.text: Incorrect CAT and Genny use can falsely show an area clear, so unrestricted use by anyone is unsafe.

D.text: A foreman's role does not automatically include locator competence; training and demonstrated skill remain necessary.

questions.prompt: If an electric drill gives off blue smoke from the motor, you should:

options.C: Switch it off and report it

questions.explanation: Defective electric hand tools must not be used. Stop what you are doing and inform your supervisor.

A.text: Water on energised equipment creates a shock path and may spread an electrical fire or damage adjacent equipment.

B.text: Cooling time does not diagnose insulation or motor failure and cannot make a smoking drill safe to restart.

C.text: Defective electric hand tools must not be used. Stop what you are doing and inform your supervisor.

D.text: An extinguisher is for an established fire; smoke from a running motor first requires isolation and defect reporting.

questions.prompt: If you only have a mains voltage (230 V) hand drill and you want to use it on a construction site which only has yellow (110 V) socket-outlets, what should you do?

options.A: Cut the plug off and fit a yellow one instead
options.B: Make up an extension cable with a yellow plug on one end and a standard socket on the other end
options.C: Obtain a 110 V drill or a cordless one for the work
options.D: Use a transformer to boost the voltage

questions.explanation: Electrical equipment must not be modified or operated at voltages other than their design voltage.

A.text: Changing only the plug exposes a 230 V drill to the wrong voltage and defeats connector coding without converting the tool.

B.text: A mixed-voltage adaptor defeats keying and can allow 230 V equipment or sockets to be misused dangerously.

C.text: Electrical equipment must not be modified or operated at voltages other than their design voltage.

D.text: A boost transformer would require a properly designed system and defeats the safer site supply; it is not an improvised solution.

questions.prompt: What hazard is created when the head of a cold chisel 'mushrooms'?
questions.explanation: This question is looking for the 'hazard', which is the situation that can cause harm to people.

A.text: The hammer may suffer secondary damage, but the brittle mushroomed rim chiefly threatens people with detached fragments.

B.text: This question is looking for the 'hazard', which is the situation that can cause harm to people.

C.text: A wider striking face affects accuracy, yet the acute injury mechanism is hardened metal breaking away at speed.

D.text: Mushrooming does not safely cushion the blow; repeated impacts work-harden and crack the spread metal edge.

questions.prompt: What precaution should you take before adjusting an electrical tool?

options.A: Check the lead is not twisted or knotted
options.C: Wear safety footwear with steel toecaps
options.D: Wear the correct personal protective equipment

questions.explanation: Disconnecting a tool from its power source before any adjustment removes all stored and supplied energy, so it cannot start unexpectedly and trap fingers or cause injury. Relying on a switch alone is not enough because it could be knocked on or fail during the work.

A.text: Lead condition matters for use, yet an untwisted lead does not isolate the tool from electrical power.

B.text: Disconnecting a tool from its power source before any adjustment removes all stored and supplied energy, so it cannot start unexpectedly and trap fingers or cause injury. Relying on a switch alone is not enough because it could be knocked on or fail during the work.

C.text: Toe protection cannot control unexpected rotation, cutting or electric shock during adjustment.

D.text: PPE may remain necessary, but it does not prevent the tool from starting while hands are at the adjustment point.

questions.prompt: A scaffold tower must be erected by:

options.C: The hire company who supply it

questions.explanation: There are a number of organizations that provide training for the safe erection and use of tower scaffolds.

A.text: There are a number of organizations that provide training for the safe erection and use of tower scaffolds.

B.text: Seniority does not demonstrate practical knowledge of the tower system, bracing sequence or stability requirements.

C.text: The supplier may erect it, but supply alone does not make that company the only competent erector.

D.text: A foreman's title does not automatically include recognised tower-scaffold training or demonstrated competence.

questions.prompt: When working on a roof that has fragile, clear-plastic panels, what is the best way of preventing falls through the panels?

options.A: Cover the fragile panels with a strong material and secure the covers to stop them being dislodged
options.B: It shouldn't be necessary to do anything, everyone knows the dangers
options.C: Make sure that everyone is told where the panels are and to avoid treading on them
options.D: Remove the panels carefully to leave an open space.

questions.explanation: Protection from falling through openings and fragile roof lights can be provided by barriers or with covers which can be secured or labelled with a warning.

questions.prompt: In an emergency situation at work you should do what?

questions.prompt: Ladders should be set at a slope of approximately:
questions.explanation: A leaning ladder should stand at roughly a one-in-four angle, meaning one unit out from the base for every four units of height. This 75-degree slope balances stability against the ladder slipping outward at the foot or tipping backward at the top.

questions.prompt: Before being used, a ladder should be inspected:

questions.prompt: Once the casualty is away from the hot metal and there is no immediate life-threatening danger, what should you do first for the hand burn?

options.A: Cover the burn with something dry
options.B: Put the hand in ice-cold water
options.C: Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes while keeping the casualty warm
options.D: Warn other people about the piece of hot metal

questions.explanation: Current NHS burns guidance is to stop the burning process and cool the affected area with cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Ice, very cold water, creams and grease can worsen injury or interfere with assessment.

A.text: A dry covering belongs after adequate cooling; applying it immediately traps residual heat in the tissue.

B.text: Ice-cold water can damage tissue and chill the casualty; use cool running water instead.

C.text: Current NHS burns guidance is to stop the burning process and cool the affected area with cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Ice, very cold water, creams and grease can worsen injury or interfere with assessment.

D.text: Warning others can follow, but it does not stop heat continuing to injure the casualty's hand.

questions.prompt: A labourer gets an electric shock; looks a bit pale but says they are alright. What should you do?

options.A: Go and check the electrics so it cannot happen again
options.B: See if they want a drink or a cigarette
options.D: Tell them to report it to their supervisor

questions.explanation: An electric shock can disturb the heart's rhythm with effects that appear minutes or hours later, so the casualty needs proper assessment even if they seem fine. Summoning the first-aider promptly ensures trained monitoring rather than assuming the person has fully recovered.

A.text: Investigating the equipment can expose another person and delays assessment of a casualty with possible internal effects.

B.text: Drink or smoking offers no treatment and may be unsafe if the casualty deteriorates or needs medical care.

C.text: An electric shock can disturb the heart's rhythm with effects that appear minutes or hours later, so the casualty needs proper assessment even if they seem fine. Summoning the first-aider promptly ensures trained monitoring rather than assuming the person has fully recovered.

D.text: Reporting to a supervisor is necessary, but the pale casualty first needs a trained health assessment.

questions.prompt: After confirming it is safe to approach an unresponsive person, what should you do when they are not breathing normally?

options.B: Call 999 or send someone to call and fetch an AED, then start CPR immediately and follow the call handler's instructions
options.C: Try to give the casualty a drink
options.D: Try to start the casualty breathing

questions.explanation: An unresponsive person who is not breathing normally may be in cardiac arrest. Activate emergency help and obtain an AED without avoidable delay, then begin CPR; broken bones and drinks are not the immediate priority.

A.text: Broken bones are secondary to absent normal breathing; circulation and oxygenation require immediate action.

B.text: An unresponsive person who is not breathing normally may be in cardiac arrest. Activate emergency help and obtain an AED without avoidable delay, then begin CPR; broken bones and drinks are not the immediate priority.

C.text: An unresponsive person can aspirate fluid and must never be given a drink.

D.text: Starting breathing is part of CPR, but calling emergency services and obtaining an AED must happen without avoidable delay.

questions.prompt: A workmate lifting a big box suddenly shouts "oh, my back" and drops the box. What should you do?

options.A: Find them somewhere comfortable to sit and rest
options.B: Help them to lift the box
options.D: Tell them to leave it for someone else to lift

questions.explanation: The priority for any back injury is to obtain first-aid advice, in order to prevent further damage.

B.text: Continuing the lift can worsen the casualty's injury and expose the helper to the same uncontrolled load.

C.text: The priority for any back injury is to obtain first-aid advice, in order to prevent further damage.

D.text: Leaving the box addresses the task but not the injured person, who still needs competent first-aid assessment.

questions.prompt: Modern portable fire extinguishers are predominantly red. How is the extinguishing medium additionally identified?

options.A: By the extinguisher's wording and a permitted colour-coded panel or band on the red body
options.B: During site induction, you will be told where the different types of extinguishers are
options.C: The type of extinguisher is written on a sign next to it
options.D: The weight and shape of the extinguisher

questions.explanation: The extinguisher label names the medium and a limited colour-coded area helps rapid identification, while the body is predominantly red. Location and shape alone are not reliable ways to choose the correct extinguisher for a fire.

A.text: The extinguisher label names the medium and a limited colour-coded area helps rapid identification, while the body is predominantly red. Location and shape alone are not reliable ways to choose the correct extinguisher for a fire.

B.text: Induction may explain locations, but memory of location does not identify an unfamiliar extinguisher in an emergency.

C.text: A nearby wall sign can be missing or obscured; identification must be carried on the extinguisher itself.

D.text: Different media can use similar cylinders, so weight and shape are not the standard identification system.

questions.prompt: When discharging carbon dioxide fire extinguishers, the nozzle:
questions.explanation: The expansion of CO2 gas coming out of the nozzle causes rapid cooling.

questions.prompt: What is a fire assembly point?

options.A: A place where fire extinguishers are kept
options.B: A place where the fire brigade goes to
options.C: The place to go when the fire alarm sounds

questions.explanation: It is essential that people go to a place of safety, where supervisors or fire marshals know where they are, in the event of a fire.

D.text: An alarm point initiates warning; it is not the place where occupants wait safely once warned.

questions.prompt: What must your employer do if the daily personal noise exposure is at or exceeds 85 db(A)?

options.A: Issue hearing protection to those exposed and ensure that it is worn
options.B: Provide hearing protection to those employees who ask for it

questions.explanation: This is an interim measure under the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 when the daily personal noise exposure is at or exceeds the upper exposure action value of 85 dB(A). Exposure should subsequently be reduced by implementing organizational or technical measures.
